APPROVED Judgment of Ms. Justice Siobhán Stack delivered 28th October, 2026.

1. Introduction

1.1

These are two related applications for relief by way of judicial review, which seek to

quash decisions of the respondent upholding earlier determinations of Fingal County Council
that certain lands comprising approximately 24.5 hectares which were zoned for residential

1

development in Portmarnock, County Dublin (variously, “the Applicants’ Lands”, “the
Lands”), satisfied the criteria for imposition of the Residential Zoned Land Tax (“RZLT”).
1.2

The purpose of the RZLT is to incentivise the development of lands which are serviced

and zoned for residential purposes, so as to encourage the provision of housing. In other words,
the objective was to prevent the hoarding of serviced lands by developers and to incentivise
the construction of residential developments.
1.3

It is not in dispute that the Applicants’ Lands are appropriately zoned, but the question

of whether those lands can be regarded as having access to the necessary services so as to fall
within the scope of the tax is hotly contested.
1.4

The RZLT was introduced by the Finance Act, 2021, which inserted a new Part 22A

(comprising ss. 653A to 653AMA) in the Taxes Consolidation Act, 1997, as amended (“the
TCA”), and is payable by landowners where their lands satisfy the criteria set out in s. 653B
(b) of the TCA. In essence, those criteria are that the land is both zoned for residential
development (including certain mixed-use zoning, which is not relevant here) and is adequately
serviced, that is, has access to the necessary public infrastructure and facilities.
1.5

In the policy documents and information leaflets published in relation to the RZLT,

lands which satisfy the statutory criteria, and which are not otherwise precluded from being
developed, are referred to as being “in scope” of the RZLT. I will use a similar shorthand in
this judgment.
1.6

There is no dispute about the fact that the Applicants’ Lands were, at all material times,

zoned for residential development: these challenges revolve around whether those Lands had
access to the necessary public infrastructure and facilities. The applicants contend that their
lands were not “in scope” at the relevant times, principally by reason of the absence of public
wastewater infrastructure in the South Portmarnock area.

2

1.7

Where lands satisfy the criteria in Part 22A as regards both zoning and access to

services, that is, where they are “in scope”, this is indicated on maps prepared by the relevant
local authority, subject to appeal by the landowners to the respondent. The Revenue
Commissioners are responsible for the administration of the tax where lands are “in scope”
but take no part in the mapping and decision-making process with which these proceedings are
concerned. For that reason, the suggestion at one point by counsel for the respondent that the
Revenue Commissioners were a necessary party to these proceedings is not, in my view,
correct.
1.8

It will be necessary to refer further below to the relevant provisions of Part 22A TCA

relating both to the process of mapping and the statutory provisions governing when lands are
regarded as being “in scope”. However, by way of context, the decisions challenged carry very
significant financial consequences for the applicants as landowners. A decision that
development lands satisfy the criteria for imposition of the RZLT renders the landowner liable
to an annual tax of 3% of the market value of the lands. This in itself is likely to be a very large
amount but, if imposed annually on foot of the annual reviews mandated by the TCA, the
amounts involved quickly run to a significant proportion of the value of the lands overall.
1.9

The earlier of the two proceedings to which this judgment relates (H.JR.2024.0001464,

“the 2024 Proceedings”) comprise a challenge to the Order of the respondent of 1 October,
2024, (“the 2024 Decision”) affirming the earlier determination of Fingal County Council
(“the Council”) dated 27 June, 2024, that the entire of the Applicants’ Lands were in scope.
The later proceedings (H.JR.2026.000160, “the 2026 Proceedings”) comprise a challenge to
the Order of the respondent of 20 November, 2025, (“the 2025 Decision”) affirming the earlier
determination of the Council dated 25 June, 2025, which is to the same effect.
